newsitem.title: UK: Sunlight can clean water, researchers say.
newsitem.headline: Sunlight can clean water, researchers say.

text.p: Sunlight can be used as a cheap and simple way to make water safe to drink, Irish doctors said on Friday.

Children who drank from plastic bottles filled with polluted water, left to sit in the hot sun, were one-third less likely to suffer diarrhoea, said Ronan Conroy of the Royal College of Surgeons in Dublin and colleagues who worked in Kenya.
Conroy said the heat and the ultraviolet radiation from the sun worked together to kill off disease-causing bacteria. The method was cheap, easy and would work almost anywhere, he said.

"It kills off more or less everything that's going," Conroy said -- E coli bacteria, cholera and other microbes. "Obviously you are not sterilising the water, but in communities that have no resources this is a real option."
Writing in the Lancet medical journal, Conroy said he and colleagues gave plastic water bottles to 206 Masai children in Kajiado province, a rural part of Kenya.
Half were told to keep the bottles on the roof of their huts and drink from them only after six hours in the sun. The other half could keep the bottles inside, in the shade.
Incidences of diarrhoea were cut by about a third in the group of children who put their bottles in the sun.
Diarrhoea is the biggest childhood threat, killing between four and six million children in the developing world every year. Clean drinking water eradicates the problem.

Conroy said the Masai were a perfect population to test the theory on as they had no access to clean water and other methods of purification, such as chlorine, would not work in the springs and wells they use.
"These children are drinking the most polluted drinking water in the world," he said.

"You drink this and I will guarantee you will be very ill. Much of it is the colour of tomato soup -- it has very fine red earth in it plus considerable quantities of cow dung plus bug counts that would turn your hair grey."
The dust in it was too fine to filter out and a lack of wood meant the water could not be boiled, he added.
But, despite a lack of controls, the sun disinfection method worked well. As societies got used to the idea, it might provide even better results.
Conroy said the idea would work in other places as well, and pointed out that plastic water bottles have become almost ubiquitous.

"Somewhere like a flood in Bangledesh where suddenly all the clean water is gone and everyone is sitting on the roof waiting for the flood to go away -- if they had the bottles they could use sunlight to try and decontaminate the floodwater."

Now Conroy said his team was now turning its attention to trachoma, another microbe-borne disease that causes blindess. He said the plastic bottle method worked there, too, when children were taught to use the disinfected water to wash in.
